newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey plays down legal challange to energy deals.
newsitem.headline: Turkey plays down legal challange to energy deals.

text.p: Turkey's power projects will go ahead as scheduled despite top court decisions which could cause significant delays in the multi-billion-dollar projects, a senior Turkish energy official said.

Mehmet Koyuncu, director of the energy affairs department at the energy ministry, said the government prepared a law to eliminate obstacles from two court rulings that two models developed to carry out big projects violated the constitution.
"The government is preparing a law to overcome court obstacles and it is going to be presented to parliament soon," he told reporters.
His comments were in response to a constitutional court ruling on Thursday that one of the models, called the build-operate-transfer (BOT), included parts violating the constitution.

The court said the BOT pattern had given the right to supervise energy projects to the government instead of the constitutional institution of the State of Council, which is the highest administrative body in Turkey.

Turkey devised the BOT model in mid-1980s to finance big infrastructure projects by foreign-led consortia with the government help in the procurement of inputs needed for the projects, for example oil, gas or water for power plants.
Projects under the model required examination by the Council of State and this caused delays for years for the projects to get the go-ahead.

To overcome such difficulties Turkey last year developed the build-operate (BO) model. Under the BO, an offshoot of BOT and to be implemented only on thermal power plant projects, the inputs should be supplied by the undertakers of the project.
But the validity of both models have been challenged by many opposition MPs and pressure groups such as the Chamber of Electrical Engineers (EMO) who said the model violated the constitution.

They have said the models gave concessions in the strategic product of electricity to private and foreign entities in breach of the constitution, which gives the control over such products only to the government.
"We will again seek the go-ahead from the Council of State although this may cause some delays," Koyuncu said. "But we will continue with all projects as scheduled," he said.
In March the State of Council rejected an energy ministry objection to a previous decision to halt the BO system being used. The case was filed at the court by EMO against the energy ministry.

Turkey, which needs urgent energy sources and has begun importing power from Iran, Bulgaria and Georgia to close deficits this year of about 2.5 billion kilowatt-hours (kWh), tendered for six gas-fired plants, several coal-fired plants and 56 hydraulic plants under both schemes.
It also invited companies to complete the constructions of and later operate 19 hydraulic power plants under the BOT scheme.
Many international companies have bid for the projects, which has an overall cost of about $10 billion.
But local companies and international bidders expressed concern over the fate of the schemes.
"There are some laws that the Turkish government should prepare for investors," said Richard Flury, executive vice president of the U.S. oil company Amoco.

"The investors should be given flexibility in investment opportunities," he told a meeting in western Izmir town for an introductory meeting of an Amoco-led partnership, which bid for two gas-fired power plants near Izmir.

Selim Yasar, president of Yasar Holding, the Turkish partner of the consortium, said the Turkish parliament should clear the obstacles and pave the way for the foreign energy investments to enter Turkey.
"The parliament should do what is expected of it in this matter," he told the same meeting. "Small obstacles should not hamper big projects," he said.
-- Ankara Newsroom, 90-312-4462940
